az-sos-2026-primary-canvass-state.note: The Secretary of State's websites refuse this site's automatic downloads, so the file was saved by hand. The canvass, certified by the Secretary of State on August 6, 2026, is a scanned paper copy with no text: its figures were read from the page images by machine, each candidate's county figures were checked to add up to the candidate's total, and every name, winner mark and total was compared by eye with the pages. The canvass prints no contest total, so a share is of all votes for the candidates in that party's primary, named write-in candidates included. The candidates the canvass marks as winners advanced; in every field they are the ones with the most votes (Arizona nominates by plurality), two in a House district and on the Corporation Commission.

measures.s:
Proposition ___ would amend the Arizona Constitution to prohibit this state and any county, city, town, municipal corporation or other political subdivision of this state from:
1. Imposing a tax or fee based on the number of miles a person travels in a motor vehicle.
2. Monitoring or limiting the number of miles a person travels in a motor vehicle, unless the person voluntarily consents.
Proposition ___ would not apply to the following:
1. The miles traveled by a person in a motor vehicle if the motor vehicle is a commercial vehicle that operates in more than one state and an interstate agreement is established for reporting fuel taxes or registration fees.
2. The miles traveled by a person in a motor vehicle if the motor vehicle is owned and operated by this state or a county, city, town, municipal corporation or other political subdivision of this state.
measures.sb: The Arizona Legislative Council (the Legislature's nonpartisan staff), in the impartial analysis A.R.S. section 19-124 requires, adopted July 8, 2026. It is printed in the Secretary of State's publicity pamphlet, not on the ballot.
measures.r: To pass, the amendment needs YES votes from a majority of the voters who vote on it. (The Arizona Constitution asks 60 percent only of an amendment that approves a tax.) (Arizona Constitution, article XXI, section 1)
measures.h: Referred to the voters by the Legislature in Senate Concurrent Resolution 1004 (2025 session), passed by the Senate on February 20, 2025 and by the House on June 13, 2025. An amendment the Legislature proposes needs a majority of the members elected to each house, and the Secretary of State then submits it at the next general election (Arizona Constitution, article XXI, section 1).

measures.s:
Proposition _____ would amend the Arizona Constitution to provide that this state and cities, towns, counties, public universities, community colleges, school districts and any other political subdivisions:
1. Are prohibited from granting preferential treatment to or discriminating against individuals or groups based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin in public employment, education or contracting, even if a part of a federal program.
2. Are prohibited from requiring applicants, employees, students or contractors to endorse or support giving preferential treatment to or discriminating against individuals based on race or ethnicity as a condition of admission, graduation, hiring, promotion, certification, contracting or other employment or scholarship opportunities. This proposition would:
(a) Prohibit requiring or soliciting a written or oral statement supporting certain race-based diversity, equity and inclusion concepts, theories or practices identified in the proposition.
(b) Prohibit requiring or soliciting individuals to confess race-based privilege or discuss the individuals' race or ethnicity or the views on or experience with the race or ethnicity of others.
(c) Prohibit giving preferable consideration to individuals based on expressed opinions if based on the race or ethnicity of those individuals.
(d) Prohibit requiring enrollment in, or completion of, any training or course that promotes the tenets outlined above.
3. Are prohibited from spending public monies to operate or contract for any office or position at a public educational institution that is responsible for promoting preferential treatment toward or discrimination against individuals or groups based on race or ethnicity, including prohibiting the use of public monies to influence the composition of the faculty and student body or for trainings, programs, activities and policies designed or implemented with reference to race, ethnicity, intersectionality, gender identity or sexual orientation, except as otherwise provided in the proposition.
4. Are prohibited from implementing any disciplinary policy or practice that treats students or employees differently on the basis of race or ethnicity.
Proposition ___ would provide for specified exceptions to these prohibitions.

measures.s:
Proposition ___ would amend the Arizona Constitution to:
1. Reaffirm that only United States citizens may register to vote and vote in Arizona elections.
2. Require voters to present valid government-issued proof of identity before casting a ballot in each election, as prescribed by law.
3. Require that voters be provided the option to have their ballots tabulated at their voting location on election day.
4. Provide that Arizona elections will be decided solely by the votes of eligible citizen voters.
5. Prohibit foreign nationals from contributing or expending money or anything of value to influence an Arizona election and any person from accepting such a contribution.
6. Allow the people and the legislature to enact laws governing elections, including early voting and mail voting, if the laws are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest, including timely and accurate election results, efficient election administration, election security and preservation of public confidence in election integrity.
7. Require the legislature to appropriate any money necessary to implement this proposition.
8. Apply this proposition to all elections that take place on or after January 1, 2028.
9. Designate this proposition as the "Fast Accurate Secure Transparent Election Results Act" or the "Fast Election Results Act."

measures.s:
Proposition ___ would limit the ability of a city, town or other taxing jurisdiction to impose a transaction privilege, sales, use, franchise or other similar tax or fee on food and certain nonalcoholic beverages (ready-to-drink and in a closed container) that are intended for home consumption as follows:
1. For a city, town or other taxing jurisdiction that approved the imposition of such a tax or fee on or before January 1, 2025, any increase in the rate of the tax or fee must be approved by the voters and may not be more than two percent of the tax base. However, if the rate of the tax or fee imposed on or before January 1, 2025 is two percent or more of the tax base, the city, town or other taxing jurisdiction may not increase the rate. Additionally, increases in the rate of the tax or fee may not occur between June 30, 2025 and June 30, 2027.
2. For a city, town or other taxing jurisdiction that has not approved the imposition of such a tax or fee on or before January 1, 2025, the adoption of a new tax or fee and any subsequent increase to the rate of the tax or fee must be approved by the voters and may not be more than two percent of the tax base. Additionally, the adoption of a new tax or fee and any subsequent increase to the rate of the tax or fee may not occur between June 30, 2025 and June 30, 2027.

measures.s:
Proposition ___ would prohibit males from playing in female interscholastic and intramural sports based on the biological sex of the participating athletes as recorded at birth on the athletes' original birth certificates. This proposition would amend Arizona law to require public and private schools and athletic associations that sponsor an interscholastic or intramural athletic team or sport to expressly designate such teams and sports as "males", "men", "boys", "females", "women", "girls", "coeducational" or "mixed".
Proposition ___ would also:
1. Prohibit public schools, private schools, higher education institutions and athletic associations that provide and maintain private spaces, including restrooms, locker rooms and shower rooms, that are integral to athletic engagement from authorizing any individual to use a private space that is not designated for that individual's biological sex as recorded at birth on the individual's original birth certificate.
2. Expand who may sue and be sued for alleged violations of the law.
3. Provide that this proposition would not restrict any athlete's eligibility to participate on a team or in a sport that is aligned with the athlete's sex or that is designated as "coeducational" or "mixed".
4. Define the term "athlete" to include students and individuals who participate in any athletic team or sport.
5. Designate this proposition as the "Protect Girls' Sports in Arizona Act."

measures.s:
Proposition ___ would require each school district that has a student count of at least 7,500 or that operates a school in a county with a population of at least 500,000 persons to spend at least 60 percent of the school district's operational spending on direct instructional expenses. The proposition would require the auditor general to define "direct instructional expenses" and "operational spending" for the purposes of this requirement.
Beginning in fiscal year 2027-2028, Proposition ___ would require any school district that spends less than 60 percent of the school district's operational spending on direct instructional expenses to increase the portion of the school district's operational spending that is spent on direct instructional expenses each year by at least one-half of one percent per year until the school district is in compliance.
If a school district does not comply with these requirements, this proposition would require the Arizona Department of Education to reduce the school district's allocation from the classroom site fund for the budget year by 25 percent of the amount that would otherwise be allocated to the school district from the classroom site fund for each year the school district did not comply, up to a maximum of 100 percent of the amount if the school district did not comply for four or more years, unless a waiver is granted. Monies that are not distributed because of reductions would be allocated to compliant school districts for the following school year.

n.t: Eight statewide propositions are shown as on the November 3, 2026 ballot, all referred by the Legislature: three constitutional amendments (141, 142, 144) and five statutes (316 to 320). The Legislative Council's table still lists eleven; the three others are explained in the notes that follow. The Secretary of State's own list and publicity pamphlet could not be read to confirm the eight.
Prop. 145 (HCR2048, military families' scholarship accounts) is off the ballot: on August 18, 2026 the Arizona Supreme Court barred the State from placing it on the November ballot.

Prop. 212 (the Protect Education Act, the only citizen initiative) is not on the ballot: the Joint Legislative Budget Committee lists it under voter initiatives not placed on the ballot, after the Arizona Supreme Court's decision order of August 18, 2026 on its petition signatures.

Prop. 143 (HCR2040, school districts and labor organizations) is not shown and not counted. News reports say a Maricopa County Superior Court judge ruled in July 2026 that it violates the separate amendment rule and that no appeal followed, and the Supreme Court's list of 2026 election cases shows no appeal for it, but no court order or Secretary of State page saying it is off the ballot could be read; its status is unconfirmed.

Arizona keeps no statewide list of local ballot questions. Each county elections department and city or town clerk prints its own (local propositions are numbered from 400 up), and the Citizens Clean Elections Commission's county pages name the local propositions each county has been told of. They are not shown here yet.

g.w: The ballot wording: official title, descriptive title, and what a "yes" and a "no" vote do (all eight propositions)
g.r: The Secretary of State sets these and prints them in the publicity pamphlet and on the ballot, but the Secretary's website could not be read here, and no other official copy has been found. The Legislature's reference title and the Legislative Council's analysis are shown instead.
Arizona law asks the Joint Legislative Budget Committee for a fiscal summary only of citizen initiatives, so none is published for these eight legislative referrals.

g.w: Whether Prop. 143 (HCR2040) is on the ballot
g.r: Reports say a superior court judge took it off the ballot in July 2026 and that there was no appeal, but neither the court's order nor the Secretary of State's list could be read to confirm it.

g.w: Local ballot questions (counties, cities, towns, school and special districts)
g.r: There is no statewide list; each county and city prints its own questions and pamphlets, and those have not been read yet.

methods: lists

Who is running comes only from the Arizona Secretary of State’s own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election and the July 21 primary, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. The November list is not loaded yet. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local races are not loaded for Arizona yet; they are loaded for 39 states so far, shown on the states page.
lists

What is read. From those lists this site reads only the office, the district, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one, and the primary vote counts. Addresses, phone numbers, e-mail and websites, where a list carries them, are never read, kept or shown. No photos, ages, biographies or campaign money are shown for state candidates.
lists
Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out.
lists

Primaries. Where more people ran in a primary (July 21) than it could send on, everyone on that primary ballot is shown, with who went on to November, read from the general election list. Vote counts are the official results where they are loaded; where they are not, the race says so.
lists
Order. Candidates appear in the ballot order the list gives, or by surname where it gives none. Never by money, polls or party.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page and nothing more.
maps

Maps and “use my location”. District lines are the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files (2024 Census Bureau cartographic boundary files), the lines the state pages draw; your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your district. Your location is worked out on your own device and never sent anywhere; a rounded copy (about half a mile) is kept on the device, with your choices, until you tap “Forget”. A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are counted only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Published polls by other pollsters that we have checked against their own release are shown apart, under Other published polls, for reference, and are never counted in the average; the rest are counted and named. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found from the Census Bureau’s 119th Congress lines, the ones the Congress pages draw, on your own device.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

changelog.title: Top movers, and breaking-news alerts for Election Night
items: Top movers: a ticker on the Forecasts page, on Election Night's Forecasts page and on the front page shows the races whose forecast moved most since the previous day's, like a stock ticker: the state, the office, the leading candidate's chance and how many points it moved, and "now leads" where the lead changed hands. Each one opens the race's chart. It stops when you point at it or move to it with the keyboard, has a Pause button, and never moves for anyone who has Motion off, Calm on or reduced motion on their device: the races then sit in a row you can scroll. Labelled Analysis.

Election Night alerts: on the night (from 4 p.m. Central on November 3), a banner across the top of every page brings the news as it comes: polls closing in each state, each state's first official results, a race whose live forecast passes 95%, a new leader in the live forecast, and projections. An early projection comes when the model gives a candidate 99% or more with at least a quarter of the expected vote counted; a full projection, in a stronger brass band, from half counted. Each says how much is counted, is labelled Analysis and "as reported, not final", and the official count decides. A projection that stops holding is withdrawn in an alert of its own. Pause, See all alerts and Close are there; nothing makes a sound; before the night the pages ask for nothing.

changelog.title: Forecasts stamped with the date and time, newest polls, ballots cast
items: Every forecast now carries the date and time it was made, so you can follow how it moved. The forecast record keeps a copy each morning until November 2, and another whenever a new run of the model changes anything, each listed by the date and time it was taken; each race's small line follows its chance from one copy to the next.

Each race's chart marks the model's earlier runs with their date and time, placed by the hour on the time line. On the Forecasts page each race says when its forecast was made, and from the standard level up a small line shows how the leading candidate's chance moved, run by run; the top of the page says when the newest run was made.

Newest polls: new polls by members of the Transparency Initiative, each checked against the pollster's own release, add 19 race results to the averages: CNN's polls by SSRS in Kansas, Maine, Michigan and Texas (Senate and governor), Emerson in Kansas, ActiVote in Texas, East Carolina University in South Carolina, Concord in South Dakota and Montana, and High Point University in North Carolina (Senate and Supreme Court). 16 results by other pollsters, in Alaska, Alabama, Iowa, Michigan, Montana, South Carolina and Texas, are shown apart and never averaged. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena polls of Minnesota and Florida, the Washington Post's of Kansas, Michigan State University's of Michigan) are listed as waiting, not shown. The poll finder no longer files a statewide poll under a House district.

Ballots cast so far: new counts from California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Maine, North Dakota, Oregon and Texas. South Dakota's newest weekly file is held back: one of its own totals does not match its party rows, so its page keeps the October 23 figures until the state corrects it.
The forecasts were made again with the new polls and counts.

changelog.title: Sandbox: Reading & access, in lanes
items: A second sandbox experiment, on the draft site only: the reading and access settings sorted into six lanes (Language, How much, Text, Colour and contrast, Motion and calm, Ready-made sets). Open a lane and its settings are tabs: click one to pin it open, as many as you like, and your pins are kept on this device. Open another lane and it opens to the left of the first, so several can be open at once; on a phone they line up in a strip you swipe through.
The Language lane comes first and names every language with a finished translation in its own words. Choosing one shows the page again in that language, with the lane still open.
The settings are the site's own, so whatever is chosen there carries to every page. Every other page still opens the usual panel.

changelog.title: Final-week polls, Texas specials, Connecticut's towns, Election Night readiness
items: Final-week polls: 32 more polls, each checked against the pollster's own release. Polls by members of the Transparency Initiative count in the averages: Marquette, Marist, Siena, Michigan State, Concord, Emerson, Targoz, ActiVote and the University of North Florida, across Senate and governor races in Wisconsin, Maine, New York, Michigan, Nebraska, Rhode Island, South Carolina and Florida, and U.S. House districts NY-17, WA-03 and KY-06. Polls by others are shown apart and never averaged; those paid for by a campaign or a party say so. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena district polls, Emerson's subscriber-only district polls) are listed as waiting, not shown. The day's forecasts were made again with them.

Texas: the state's November 3 special elections for State House District 93 and State Senate District 22, the 276th District Court, a Democrat added to one judicial race, and nine declared write-ins are now on Texas's ballot pages, from the Secretary of State's own lists.

Connecticut: every town has now posted its sample ballot, and all are read: registrars of voters, town and school board contests, and every probate district now carry their candidates (110 local races, up from 76).

On state ballot pages, 43 kinds of local office that were listed at the end under their own titles (Florida's community development boards, library boards, receivers of taxes and others) now sit with the offices like them.

Election Night: Minnesota's saved results files are read about four times faster; Texas's two special elections and its judicial race are tied to the state's results; a new check holds back any state's file that shows votes before its polls close (three states' test files do today); and practice runs can no longer reach the public results.
Election Night counts 267 statewide races, and the U.S. page now names the District of Columbia's two offices apart from them. The Past results door now says all 50 states and DC are loaded.

State ballot pages: Georgia's and Virginia's mail-ballot notes no longer call October 23 "this Friday"; notes and source lines no longer describe how this site reads its files or show raw web addresses (each source's link is still there).

Wording: the news-outlet count now matches everywhere; the Method page says plainly that polls outside our average are shown apart; it says which Forecasts page lists every forecast; the privacy answers now name the Forecasts page's address look-up and street maps, and the Access page names the weather picture's one request; the page guide no longer says Minnesota is the only state with a forecast map.

changelog.title: A sandbox, and Anthropic's prospectus four ways
items: A sandbox on the draft site, for experiments: in no menu, not on the live site, and every page asks search engines not to list it.

Its first experiment is the prospectus Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, filed with the SEC on October 26, 2026, four ways. As filed: a link to the official copy on SEC.gov. In chapters: save the official copy from SEC.gov and open it in a reader that rebuilds it into its 27 chapters, with highlights, notes, search, a page-by-page view as filed, and a PDF of a chapter, the chapters you marked, your notes alone or the whole filing. The copy and your notes stay on your device; this site never holds the filing's text. In five minutes: about 1,230 words in the filing's own order, in our words, checked claim by claim against the filing. And an analysis of whether it reads as if an AI wrote it: whether text carries a mark that says so (it does not, for anyone to read), and the word counts studies tie to AI writing, beside eight other prospectuses, four of them filed before ChatGPT existed. Every figure there is labelled Analysis and says what it cannot tell you.
The pages say the site is built with the help of Claude, and that Anthropic had no part in them.

Ballots cast so far: California, South Dakota, Colorado, Louisiana, Oregon and South Carolina are current again, read from the new names and layouts their offices now use. Iowa's site now refuses programs and Washington shows its counts only inside a dashboard, so both wait for a hand-saved copy; Oklahoma has not posted yet. Building these pages takes under a second, down from half an hour.

changelog.title: Every state on the forecast map
items: Each state on both Forecasts pages now has its map and "Your ballot, as forecast", with Share: all 40 states with a forecast, not Minnesota alone. Use your location or type your address, and the page lists every race on your ballot there with the model's forecast where it has one. Your location stays on your device.
A state's map and its list of races load only when you open that state.
In the states that drew new congressional lines for 2026, the map says so, and your U.S. House district is found only from the new lines, never the old ones.

The nine states with new U.S. House districts for 2026 (Alabama, California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas, Utah) now show those districts on the ballot maps, from the Census Bureau's 2026 plan files published October 6, and "Use my location" or a typed address finds your 2026 district there. Before, those maps showed only the state's outline.

A statewide board elected by district (Texas's State Board of Education and others) is no longer put on every ballot in the state: it is placed by its own district, or the page says it cannot tell which seat is yours.
Past results load from the site's own results store rather than from each copy of the site, which leaves more room for election week.

Where a state's precinct lines are not on file here, your ballot still lists its statewide races. A statewide board elected by district (a state board of education, a public service commission) is no longer put on every ballot in the state: it is counted among the races the page could not place, and the state's own ballot lookup is the authority.

attorney_general.t: The attorney general is the state's top lawyer. The office speaks for the state in court, advises state agencies and enforces consumer laws.
s: About Our Office, Minnesota Attorney General
About the Office of Attorney General, Arizona Attorney General

x.es: El procurador general es el principal abogado del estado. La oficina representa al estado ante los tribunales, asesora a las agencias estatales y hace cumplir las leyes de protección al consumidor.

governor.t: The governor is the state's top leader. The governor signs or vetoes new laws, names many state officials and leads the state's military forces.
s: Texas Constitution, Article 4 (Executive Department), Texas Legislature
Michigan Constitution of 1963, Article V (Executive Branch), Michigan Legislature

x.es: El gobernador es el líder principal del estado. El gobernador firma o veta las nuevas leyes, nombra a muchos funcionarios estatales y dirige las fuerzas militares del estado.

secretary_of_state.t: In most states, the secretary of state runs elections and keeps records, such as business filings. Other duties differ by state.
s: Secretary of State Divisions & Programs, Nebraska Secretary of State

x.es: En la mayoría de los estados, el secretario de estado administra las elecciones y guarda registros, como los documentos que presentan las empresas. Las demás funciones varían según el estado.

state_house.t: The state House (called the Assembly or House of Delegates in some states) is the larger chamber. Its members write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Q&A, Colorado House of Representatives

x.es: La Cámara de Representantes del estado (llamada Asamblea o Cámara de Delegados en algunos estados) es la cámara más grande. Sus miembros redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

state_mine_inspector.t: This office checks mines in Arizona for safety and looks into mine accidents. It can also inspect old mines no longer in use.
s: Arizona Revised Statutes 27-124, Mine inspections required; powers of inspector, Arizona Legislature
Arizona Revised Statutes 27-121, State mine inspector, Arizona Legislature

x.es: Este cargo revisa la seguridad de las minas de Arizona e investiga los accidentes en las minas. También puede inspeccionar minas viejas que ya no se usan.

state_senate.t: The state Senate is the smaller of the Legislature's two chambers (Nebraska has only one). Senators write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Branch Function and Process, North Dakota Legislative Branch

x.es: El Senado estatal es la más pequeña de las dos cámaras de la Legislatura (Nebraska tiene solo una). Los senadores redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

state_treasurer.t: The state treasurer keeps the state's money safe. The office takes in and invests state money, pays it out, and in many states returns lost money to its owners.
s: Illinois Constitution, Article V, Section 18 (Treasurer - duties), Illinois General Assembly

x.es: El tesorero estatal guarda de forma segura el dinero del estado. La oficina recibe e invierte el dinero del estado, hace los pagos y, en muchos estados, devuelve el dinero perdido a sus dueños.

superintendent_of_public_instruction.t: This office runs the state's school agency. It hands out school money, gives statewide tests and licenses teachers.
s: About Us, Idaho Department of Education
About Us, North Dakota Department of Public Instruction
About the State Department of Education, Oklahoma.gov

x.es: Este cargo dirige la agencia escolar del estado. Reparte el dinero para las escuelas, aplica exámenes en todo el estado y otorga licencias a los maestros.
